title: What If a Nuclear Reactor Fell From Orbit? One Hit Canada in 1978

scenes.text: What if a nuclear reactor fell from orbit? One did in 1978. The bill was never paid.
Kosmos 954 was a Soviet spy satellite powered by a reactor holding 50 kilograms of enriched uranium. In December 1977, it stopped obeying.
January 24, 1978. It re-enters over northern Canada and breaks apart. Radioactive debris rains along a 600-kilometer path.
Teams search 124,000 square kilometers. Some fragments on the ice of Great Slave Lake could kill a person in a few hours.
The most radioactive piece is a flake the size of a nickel. In the end they recover about one percent of the fuel.
Canada billed Moscow six million dollars. The Soviets paid half. Nobody was hurt, only because it fell on one of the emptiest places on Earth.

description:
What if a nuclear-powered satellite crashed to Earth? On 24 January 1978 the Soviet spy satellite Kosmos 954, carrying a reactor with about 50 kg of highly enriched uranium, re-entered over northern Canada and scattered radioactive debris along a roughly 600 km path from Great Slave Lake toward Baker Lake.
Operation Morning Light searched more than 124,000 square kilometres with over 4,500 flight hours; some core fragments were radioactive enough to be lethal after a few hours of contact, yet only about 1 percent of the fuel was ever recovered. Canada billed the USSR about 6 million dollars for the clean-up and received about 3 million. No one was injured.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: The Soviets had quietly warned the Americans weeks earlier that they had lost control of it. What should fall from orbit next in our thought experiments? Drop your own what-if below.
